specStatements.text: The transition elements are metals with similar properties which are different from those of the elements in Group 1.
Students should be able to describe the difference compared with Group 1 in melting points, densities, strength, hardness and reactivity with oxygen, water and halogens.
Students should be able to exemplify these general properties by reference to Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu.
Many transition elements have ions with different charges, form coloured compounds and are useful as catalysts.
Students should be able to exemplify these general properties by reference to compounds of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu.

scopeNotes.statement: Exemplification is limited to Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and no explanation of why the properties differ is required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every transition element used to illustrate melting point, density, strength, hardness or reactivity is one of the six the specification names: chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel and copper. Comparisons are made only against Group 1 metals, and no electronic structure is used to explain why the properties differ.

scopeNotes.statement: Exemplification is limited to compounds of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and no explanation of colour or of catalytic action is required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Ion charges, compound colours and catalytic uses are illustrated only with compounds of chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel and copper. Students are asked to state and use these properties, never to explain why d-block ions are coloured or why they catalyse reactions.

concepts.definition: The metals in the central block of the periodic table, between Group 2 and Group 3. They have properties that are similar to one another and different from the properties of the Group 1 metals.

The metals in the first column of the periodic table, such as lithium, sodium and potassium. They are soft, have low melting points and low densities, and react quickly with water, with oxygen and with the halogens.

Transition elements have much higher melting points than Group 1 metals. Chromium melts at about 1907 degrees C and iron at about 1538 degrees C, while sodium melts at about 98 degrees C and potassium at about 63 degrees C.

Transition elements are much denser than Group 1 metals. Copper is about 8.9 g/cm3 and nickel about 8.9 g/cm3, while sodium is about 0.97 g/cm3, which is less than the density of water, so sodium floats.

Transition elements such as chromium, iron, cobalt and nickel are hard and strong, which is why they are used for tools, machinery and hard-wearing chrome plating. Group 1 metals are soft enough to be cut with a knife.

Group 1 metals react with cold water, fizzing as hydrogen is released. Transition elements react very slowly or not at all with cold water, which is why copper is used for water pipes and why iron only rusts slowly in damp air.

A freshly cut Group 1 metal loses its shine within seconds as it reacts with oxygen in the air. Transition elements react far more slowly: copper stays shiny for months, and only turns black when it is heated strongly in air.

Group 1 metals react vigorously with the halogens. Transition elements react much less readily and usually need heating: hot iron reacts with chlorine to form iron(III) chloride, 2Fe + 3Cl2 gives 2FeCl3.
Many transition elements form more than one ion. Iron forms Fe2+ and Fe3+, copper forms Cu+ and Cu2+, and chromium forms Cr2+ and Cr3+, whereas a Group 1 metal only ever forms a 1+ ion.

Compounds of transition elements are usually coloured: copper(II) sulfate is blue, iron(II) sulfate is pale green, iron(III) oxide is red-brown, nickel(II) compounds are green and potassium manganate(VII) is purple. Group 1 compounds are usually white and give colourless solutions.

A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up in the reaction. Many transition elements and their compounds are catalysts: iron in the Haber process, nickel for hardening vegetable oils, and manganese(IV) oxide for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

The Roman numeral in a name such as iron(II) chloride or manganese(IV) oxide gives the charge on the metal ion, not the number of atoms in the formula. Iron(II) chloride is FeCl2 and iron(III) chloride is FeCl3.

misconceptions.question: Does nickel fizz in cold water in the way that potassium does?
misconceptions.correct: Potassium reacts vigorously with cold water and fizzes as hydrogen is given off. Nickel shows no visible reaction with cold water at all.
misconceptions.misconception: All metals react with cold water and fizz; transition metals simply do it a little more slowly than the Group 1 metals do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reactivity series is met as a single ranked list, which makes reactivity look like a difference of speed rather than a difference of whether anything happens at all. Rusting is also described as iron reacting with water, so students expect iron and water to react on contact.
misconceptions.correction: Group 1 metals react with cold water on contact. Transition elements such as chromium, nickel and copper react extremely slowly or not at all, which is why copper is used for water pipes. Rusting needs water and oxygen together over days, not seconds.

misconceptions.question: Iron is harder and stronger than sodium. Does that make iron the more reactive metal?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sodium is far more reactive than iron, even though sodium is soft enough to be cut with a knife.
misconceptions.misconception: A hard, strong, heavy metal must also be a powerful, reactive one, so transition metals react more fiercely than Group 1 metals do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language 'strong' and 'powerful' describe the same thing, and students carry that over into chemistry. The transition metals are also the ones seen doing heavy work in bridges and engines, which reinforces the idea that they are the aggressive ones.
misconceptions.correction: Hardness and strength are physical properties; reactivity is a chemical property, and the two are separate. Group 1 metals are soft, weak and extremely reactive, while transition elements are hard, strong and much less reactive.

misconceptions.question: Sodium melts at 98 degrees C. Is that a printing error?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sodium really does melt at about 98 degrees C, which is below the boiling point of water.
misconceptions.misconception: All metals melt at around a thousand degrees or more, because that is simply what metals are like.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The metals students meet in workshops and in industry are steels and copper alloys, all of which need furnace temperatures to melt. Group 1 metals are only ever seen stored under oil, so their low melting points are never experienced directly.
misconceptions.correction: Group 1 metals have low melting points, and they fall down the group: lithium 180 degrees C, sodium 98 degrees C, potassium 63 degrees C. Transition elements melt far higher: iron 1538 degrees C and chromium 1907 degrees C.

misconceptions.question: A piece of sodium floats on water. Does that mean it is not really a metal?
misconceptions.correct: It is a metal. Sodium has a density of about 0.97 g/cm3, which is less than the 1.0 g/cm3 of water, so it floats.
misconceptions.misconception: Every metal is denser than water and must sink, so anything that floats cannot be a metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every metal a student handles day to day is dense, and being heavy is treated as part of the definition of a metal. Density is also often confused with how heavy an object feels rather than mass per unit volume.
misconceptions.correction: Group 1 metals have low densities, and lithium, sodium and potassium all float on water. Transition elements are much denser: copper and nickel are both about 8.9 g/cm3 and sink immediately.

misconceptions.question: Iron forms Fe2+ and Fe3+. Are these two different elements?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both are iron, with 26 protons. Fe2+ is an iron atom that has lost two electrons and Fe3+ one that has lost three.
misconceptions.misconception: If the charge is different then something in the nucleus must be different, so Fe3+ has a different number of protons from Fe2+.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge is first met when defining protons and electrons, and proton number is stressed as the thing that fixes which element you have. Students then reach for the nucleus whenever a charge changes, instead of for the outer electrons.
misconceptions.correction: Ion charge comes from electrons lost or gained; proton number never changes in a chemical reaction. A transition element can lose different numbers of electrons, which is exactly why it forms ions with different charges.

misconceptions.question: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue. Are all sulfate solutions blue?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sodium sulfate solution is colourless. The blue comes from the copper ion, not from the sulfate ion.
misconceptions.misconception: The non-metal part of a compound carries the colour, so every sulfate is blue and every chloride is white.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper(II) sulfate is the first coloured salt most students meet, and it is met so often that its colour becomes attached to the word 'sulfate'. Names are also read left to right, so the last-named part feels like the important one.
misconceptions.correction: In these compounds the colour comes from the transition metal ion. Copper(II) sulfate is blue, iron(II) sulfate is pale green and sodium sulfate is white, yet all three contain the same sulfate ion.

misconceptions.question: Manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide. Is it used up as the oxygen is given off?
misconceptions.correct: No. The manganese(IV) oxide can be filtered off at the end, dried and used again.
misconceptions.misconception: The catalyst is one of the ingredients, so it is consumed like the other reactants and has to be replaced each time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Anything added to a reaction vessel looks like a reactant, and students see the catalyst mixed in with everything else. Industrial catalysts do have to be replaced eventually, which is often mentioned and then over-generalised.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up by it. It does not appear in the balanced equation, and it can be recovered unchanged in mass at the end of the reaction.

misconceptions.question: In iron(II) chloride, does the (II) mean there are two chlorine atoms?
misconceptions.correct: No. It means the iron ion has a charge of 2+. Two chloride ions are then needed to balance that charge.
misconceptions.misconception: The Roman numeral is a way of counting the atoms of the other element in the formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: For iron(II) chloride the numeral and the number of chlorine atoms happen to coincide, so the wrong rule gives the right formula and is never challenged. It then fails on compounds such as manganese(IV) oxide, MnO2.
misconceptions.correction: The Roman numeral always gives the charge on the metal ion. Manganese(IV) oxide contains a 4+ manganese ion but only two oxygen atoms, MnO2, which shows that the numeral is not an atom count.

misconceptions.question: Copper does not react with cold water. Does that mean it never reacts with oxygen or with chlorine?
misconceptions.correct: It does react, but slowly, or only when heated. Copper heated in air turns black, and heated iron reacts with chlorine.
misconceptions.misconception: Transition metals are the unreactive metals, so they do not react with oxygen or with the halogens at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper pipes and stainless steel cutlery survive for years, so these metals are experienced as inert. The word 'unreactive' is then treated as an absolute rather than as a comparison with Group 1.
misconceptions.correction: Transition elements are less reactive than Group 1 metals, not unreactive. They react with oxygen and with halogens more slowly, and usually need heating, but the reactions do happen.

misconceptions.question: Does every metal ion have one fixed charge?
misconceptions.correct: No. Group 1 metals always form 1+ ions, but many transition elements form ions with more than one charge.
misconceptions.misconception: A metal has one charge that never changes, so iron is always Fe2+ in the way that sodium is always Na+.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ionic bonding is taught first with Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7, where the charge is fixed by the group number. That rule is powerful and gets applied to the whole periodic table, including the block where it does not hold.
misconceptions.correction: The group-number rule works for the main groups only. Transition elements form ions with different charges, which is why their names carry a Roman numeral: iron(II) and iron(III), copper(I) and copper(II).

misconceptions.question: Does adding a catalyst increase the mass of product you finally obtain?
misconceptions.correct: No. It gets you to the same amount of product faster; the amount made at the end is not increased.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst improves the reaction, so it must increase how much product you end up with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Speeds up' and 'improves' merge into one vague idea of making the reaction better, and industrial catalysts are described as making a process more productive, which is about time rather than amount.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst changes the rate only. The amount of product is fixed by the amounts of reactant and by the balanced equation, so a catalyst gets you there sooner, not further.

misconceptions.question: Are all metal compounds white solids?
misconceptions.correct: No. Group 1 compounds are usually white, but transition metal compounds are usually coloured.
misconceptions.misconception: Compounds are white crystals like salt, so transition metal compounds are white too and dissolve to give colourless solutions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium chloride is the model compound in almost every lesson on ionic bonding, and the compounds handled in early practical work are mostly white powders, so being white becomes part of what a compound is.
misconceptions.correction: Transition metal compounds are usually coloured, both as solids and in solution: copper(II) sulfate blue, nickel(II) sulfate green, iron(III) oxide red-brown, potassium manganate(VII) purple.

misconceptions.question: Sodium melts easily. Does that also tell you it has a low density?
misconceptions.correct: Both happen to be true for sodium, but one does not follow from the other. Melting point and density are separate properties.
misconceptions.misconception: A metal that melts at a low temperature must also be a light metal, because melting point and density measure much the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both properties are used to sort metals into 'soft light ones' and 'tough heavy ones', so students bundle them into a single idea instead of treating them as two independent measurements.
misconceptions.correction: Density is mass per unit volume; melting point is the temperature at which a solid turns liquid. Mercury has a very low melting point and a very high density, which shows that the two are independent.

misconceptions.question: Copper metal is red-brown. Should copper(II) sulfate solution be red-brown too?
misconceptions.correct: No. Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue, even though the metal it comes from is red-brown.
misconceptions.misconception: A compound shows the colour of the metal it is made from, so the colour of the metal tells you the colour of the compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour is treated as a fixed possession of a substance rather than a property of the particles present, so it is transferred from element to compound without any expectation that it will change.
misconceptions.correction: The colour belongs to the ion, not to the metal. Copper metal is red-brown while copper(II) ions in solution are blue, and iron metal is grey while iron(III) oxide is red-brown.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the transition elements when they are compared with the Group 1 metals?

options.text: They react with water and with oxygen far more violently than Group 1 metals
options.rationale: Students who treat reactivity as one continuous scale, and who know the transition metals are the tough ones, expect them to react harder with everything.

options.text: They have properties that are similar to each other but different from Group 1 metals
options.rationale: The specification states that the transition elements are metals with similar properties which are different from those of the elements in Group 1.

options.text: They each behave differently, so this block shares no common properties
options.rationale: Seeing that iron forms both Fe2+ and Fe3+ suggests unpredictability, so students conclude the block follows no shared pattern at all.

options.text: They have the same properties as Group 1 metals but higher atomic numbers
options.rationale: Students who know both sets are metals assume that being a metal fixes the properties, and that position in the table only changes the atomic number.

mcqs.stem: Sodium melts at 98 degrees C and chromium melts at 1907 degrees C. Which conclusion do these values support?

options.text: The sodium sample was impure, because every metal melts well above 1000 degrees C
options.rationale: Students who believe all metals need furnace temperatures explain the low value away as a fault in the sample rather than accept it as a real property.

options.text: Chromium melts higher because it is the more reactive metal of the two
options.rationale: Reactivity and physical toughness are merged, so the harder metal is expected to win on every measure, including melting point.

options.text: Melting point depends only on mass, so a heavier atom melts higher
options.rationale: A rule that fits this one pair is over-generalised; it fails at once for mercury, which is heavy yet is liquid at room temperature.

options.text: Transition elements usually melt at much higher temperatures than Group 1 metals
options.rationale: This is the melting point difference the specification asks students to describe, and chromium against sodium is a clear example of it.

mcqs.stem: A small piece of sodium floats on water, but a small piece of copper sinks. What does this show?

options.text: Sodium is less dense than water, while copper is far denser than water
options.rationale: Sodium is about 0.97 g/cm3 and copper about 8.9 g/cm3, which is the density difference between Group 1 and the transition elements.

options.text: Sodium cannot be a true metal, because every metal is denser than water is
options.rationale: Students who treat being heavy as part of the definition of a metal reject the observation rather than accept a metal with a low density.

options.text: Sodium melts at a low temperature, so a metal that melts easily is light
options.rationale: Melting point and density are bundled into a single idea of soft light metals, so one property is offered as the reason for the other.

options.text: Copper sinks because it is the harder and stronger of these metals
options.rationale: Hardness, strength and density are treated as one property of toughness, so hardness is given as the reason for sinking.

mcqs.stem: Potassium and nickel are each added to a separate beaker of cold water. What would you see?

options.text: Both metals fizz gently, but the nickel fizzes much more slowly
options.rationale: The reactivity series read as a speed scale means every metal reacts with water, with the less reactive one simply taking longer.

options.text: Neither metal changes, because cold water is far too cold to react
options.rationale: Students who remember that many metal reactions need heating apply that to Group 1 as well, and expect nothing at room temperature.

options.text: Potassium fizzes and melts; the nickel does not change
options.rationale: Potassium reacts vigorously with cold water, releasing hydrogen and melting from the heat given out, while nickel shows no visible reaction.

options.text: The nickel fizzes strongly while the potassium slowly darkens
options.rationale: Learners who equate the hard, tough metal with the powerful one reverse the two observations completely.

mcqs.stem: Freshly cut sodium and freshly polished copper are both left out in air. What happens to their shiny surfaces?

options.text: The copper stays shiny for ever, because it never reacts with oxygen
options.rationale: Copper pipes and coins last for years, so students take less reactive to mean that no reaction with oxygen is possible at all.

options.text: The sodium stays shiny, while the copper dulls in a few seconds
options.rationale: Students who expect the hard, heavy metal to be the aggressive one swap the two observations round.

options.text: Both dull at the same rate, since both of them react with oxygen
options.rationale: Knowing that both metals do react with oxygen is taken to mean they react at the same rate, which ignores the size of the difference.

options.text: The sodium dulls within seconds; the copper only dulls slowly over months
options.rationale: A cut surface of sodium is coated with oxide almost at once, whereas copper reacts with oxygen very slowly unless it is heated strongly.

mcqs.stem: Sodium and iron are each heated in chlorine gas. Which statement about these two reactions is correct?

options.text: Sodium reacts violently, while iron reacts less readily to give FeCl3
options.rationale: Group 1 metals react vigorously with halogens; hot iron reacts less readily, forming iron(III) chloride, 2Fe + 3Cl2 gives 2FeCl3.

options.text: Iron reacts far more violently, because it is the harder, stronger metal
options.rationale: Physical toughness is read as chemical power, so iron is expected to overwhelm sodium in any reaction it takes part in.

options.text: Only sodium reacts, as transition metals never react with halogens
options.rationale: Treating less reactive as inert makes students rule the iron reaction out entirely, even though it is a standard demonstration.

options.text: Both react at the same rate, because chlorine is very reactive
options.rationale: The reactivity of the non-metal is treated as the only thing that matters, so the difference between the two metals is ignored.

mcqs.stem: Element X melts at 1495 degrees C, has a density of 8.9 g/cm3 and shows no reaction with cold water. Which element is X most likely to be?

options.text: Sodium, because metals such as sodium melt at above 1000 degrees C
options.rationale: Believing that all metals melt very high, a student sees the high melting point as no obstacle to the answer being a Group 1 metal.

options.text: Lithium, because all metals are dense and sink in water
options.rationale: A student convinced that metals must be dense reads 8.9 g/cm3 as normal for any metal, so it does not rule lithium out.

options.text: Cobalt, because those values are typical of a transition metal
options.rationale: Cobalt melts at 1495 degrees C and has a density of 8.9 g/cm3; a high melting point, high density and no reaction with cold water are the transition metal pattern.

options.text: Calcium, because it reacts only slowly with the cold water in a beaker
options.rationale: A slow reaction is treated as the same thing as no reaction, so a metal that does fizz in cold water is still accepted.

mcqs.stem: Which set of properties is typical of many of the transition elements?

options.text: One fixed ion charge, white compounds and use as catalysts
options.rationale: The group-number rule for ionic charge is carried across the whole table, and salt is taken as the model for what a compound looks like.

options.text: Ions of different charges, coloured compounds, catalysts
options.rationale: The specification states that many transition elements have ions with different charges, form coloured compounds and are useful as catalysts.

options.text: Ions of different charges, white compounds and low densities
options.rationale: The variable charge is recalled correctly, but compounds are still assumed to be white and the Group 1 low density is carried over.

options.text: One fixed ion charge, coloured compounds and low melting points
options.rationale: The colour is recalled, but the fixed charge and the low melting points actually belong to the Group 1 metals.

mcqs.stem: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue, but sodium sulfate solution is colourless. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Copper is a transition element, and its compounds are usually coloured
options.rationale: Forming coloured compounds is one of the properties the specification gives for transition elements, exemplified here by a compound of copper.

options.text: The sulfate ion gives the blue colour in any sulfate solution
options.rationale: Copper(II) sulfate is met so often that its colour becomes attached to the word sulfate rather than to the copper ion.

options.text: Sodium compounds are coloured too, but much too faintly to see
options.rationale: Rather than accept two different kinds of compound, students assume every compound is coloured and that some colours are simply weak.

options.text: The solution is blue because copper metal itself is blue
options.rationale: Colour is treated as a fixed possession of the element, so the compound is expected to look like the metal; copper metal is in fact red-brown.

mcqs.stem: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl2 and FeCl3. What does the (II) in the name iron(II) chloride tell you?

options.text: Two chlorine atoms are joined to each of the iron atoms
options.rationale: For this compound the numeral matches the number of chlorine atoms, so the wrong rule gives the right formula and survives unchallenged.

options.text: The iron atom has lost two protons from the nucleus
options.rationale: Charge is linked to the nucleus rather than to electrons lost, so a 2+ charge is read as a change in proton number.

options.text: It is the second of the chlorides that iron forms
options.rationale: The numeral is read as a serial label counting compounds in a list, which happens to fit iron but fails for manganese(IV) oxide.

options.text: The iron ion in this compound carries a charge of 2+
options.rationale: The Roman numeral gives the charge on the transition metal ion, which is what lets iron form both iron(II) and iron(III) compounds.

mcqs.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly. When manganese(IV) oxide is added, oxygen is given off quickly. What is the manganese(IV) oxide doing?

options.text: It is used up in the reaction, so more must be added each time
options.rationale: Anything added to the flask looks like a reactant, so the catalyst is assumed to be consumed along with the peroxide.

options.text: It speeds up the reaction and is not itself used up
options.rationale: Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst, one of the uses of transition metal compounds that the specification names.

options.text: It raises the total volume of oxygen that can be given off
options.rationale: Speeding up and improving are merged, so the catalyst is credited with increasing the amount of product rather than the rate.

options.text: It reacts with the peroxide to release the oxygen
options.rationale: The gas appears as soon as the solid is added, which makes the solid look like the source of the oxygen rather than a catalyst.

mcqs.stem: Sodium can be cut with a knife, but chromium is used for tools and hard-wearing plating. What does this show?

options.text: Chromium is harder, so it is also the more reactive of the two
options.rationale: Hardness is a physical property and reactivity a chemical one. Sodium is far more reactive than chromium, even though it is soft.

options.text: Transition elements are hard and strong, while Group 1 metals are soft
options.rationale: This is the strength and hardness difference the specification asks students to describe, shown here by chromium against sodium.

options.text: Sodium is too soft to be counted as a proper metal at all
options.rationale: Sodium is a metal: it is shiny when cut and conducts electricity. Being soft is one of its properties, not a reason to exclude it.

options.text: Hardness, density and melting point are really one single property
options.rationale: Metals get sorted into soft light ones and tough heavy ones, bundling separate properties. Mercury is dense yet liquid at room temperature.
